doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Avant garde in Europe versus America today
summary: Rowe asks about under-represented ends of jazz; Ali says avant garde is popular in Europe and alive but not well in America.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You know you were talking the other day, I guess yesterday, about the effort that you made, both of you, back a number of years ago to get free or avant garde jazz on some of these festivals, that they weren’t presenting that spectrum of the music. And in the last year or so I went to a big jazz convention and the people that promote Dixieland music, or very early, were complaining about the same thing. And it’s like they’re leaving out the ends of the music. Do you agree with that? And can you tell me about —

Well back, like in the 70s, like the early part of the 70s, I don’t know too much about the Dixieland but probably all even Dixieland and avant garde now, but not now, not so much now, because the avant garde is really popular in Europe. And I mean you know we get like huge crowds in Europe with this stuff. And it’s festivals attracts a lot of people from all around. But actually it really got a hold there more or less more so than here. In fact, most of the European players that play jazz are into avant garde more than anything else. Some of the fusion stuff works too a little bit, you know, like the cut from the “Bitches Brew” era, and stuff, but a lot of the music is very avant garde there in Europe. And so like here, in America, it’s alive but not well. You know it’s alive here. You can find this stuff in just about every major city.
